did_you_know.text: Bowing seven times was a gesture of honor and submission known in the ancient world. Jacob uses it to show his desire to make peace with Esau.
The Torah has dots above the word “and he kissed him,” as if inviting special attention to this kiss. The Sages debated whether Esau kissed Jacob sincerely or meant to bite him.

The phrase “I have seen your face like the face of God” connects with the name Peniel, which Jacob gave the place after his nighttime struggle. Jacob describes meeting Esau as frightening, yet also life-saving.
In Biblical Hebrew, the word “blessing” can also mean a gift, not only a good wish. Jacob is therefore asking Esau to accept the gifts he brought him.
Jacob understands that young children and herds cannot travel at the pace of strong, fast travelers. His words show the practical responsibility of a shepherd to care for everyone who depends on him.
The name Sukkot is connected with temporary shelters Jacob built for the animals. This is the first place in the Bible called by that name, long before the commandment of the festival of Sukkot.
The word “shalem” can mean “safely” or “in wholeness,” but some interpreters understand it as the name of a place. That is why translations begin this verse in different ways.
